articles.title: India and China aren't friends - but Nepal wants to unite them against climate threats
articles.summary: Can Nepal bring the two regional giants together to confront a shared climate threat in the Himalayas?
articles.full_text:
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
The recent floods in Nepal have highlighted the need for cross-border co-operation in the Himalayan region By Navin Singh Khadka Environment correspondent, BBC World Service 
- Published 47 minutes ago 
Nepal's Prime Minister Balendra Shah used much of his speech at the recent UN General Assembly to warn of the growing threat of climate-related disasters in the Himalayas, recalling the devastating debris floods that struck his country in August. 
But it was his ambitious proposal to bring together regional rivals India and China, alongside Nepal, to tackle these shared threats that drew particular attention. 
Shah called for the creation of a Himalayan Climate Resilience Mechanism to strengthen cross-border disaster response and the sharing of scientific data and expertise in one of the world's most environmentally fragile and geopolitically sensitive regions. 
"Let the Himalayas become a laboratory of international co-operation rather than a frontier of fragmented information," he said. 
A senior official at Nepal's foreign ministry, speaking on condition of anonymity, said the proposal was still at an early stage. 
"The PM's proposal has given a political direction. Our ministry is working with other relevant agencies to put forward a preliminary framework which can be the basis for building common understanding," the official said. 
Neither India nor China has formally responded to the proposal. The BBC has contacted their foreign ministries for comment. 
But can Nepal really bring the two regional giants together to confront a shared climate threat in a region where they have long been locked in bitter territorial disputes? 
India and China share a disputed frontier stretching roughly 3,500km (2,175 miles), much of it across the Himalayas. Their competing territorial claims have led to a war, deadly clashes and repeated military stand-offs along the Line of Actual Control (LAC), the de facto boundary separating areas under their control. 
But the mountains that have long been a source of friction between the two countries are also facing an urgent climate threat. 
Temperatures in the Himalayan region are rising faster than the global average, accelerating glacier retreat and permafrost thaw and contributing to growing risks of landslides, rockfalls, avalanches and glacial lake outburst floods. 
Such disasters can sweep across national boundaries, threatening lives, infrastructure and livelihoods far downstream - making co-operation between the countries sharing the Himalayas increasingly important. 
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
Balendra Shah has urged neighbours India and China to collaborate on climate risks in the Himalayan region 
A report by the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development , external released in March found that glaciers across the Hindu Kush Himalaya (HKH) region are melting at an accelerating pace, with the rate of ice loss having doubled since 2000 compared with the 1974-1999 period. 
Further east, on the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau, glaciers have shrunk by 24% in area over the past six decades, Kang Shichang, director of the Chinese Academy of Sciences' Institute of Mountain Hazards and Environment, told China's People's Daily Online. 
Experts say the retreat of glaciers can cause glacial lakes to expand, increasing the risk of sudden, potentially devastating floods that can cross borders into countries such as Nepal, India and Bhutan. Several major rivers flowing through these countries originate on the Tibetan Plateau. 
The plateau now has more than 14,000 glacial lakes, covering over 1,100 sq km, according to People's Daily. 
And the dangers extend beyond flooding. 
A 2024 study published by the American Geophysical Union projected a significant rise in landslide hazards across the Himalayas and Tibet in the coming decades due to increased rainstorms. 
While the largest absolute increases are expected in already vulnerable areas, including India's Garhwal and Kumaon regions and Nepal, the greatest relative increase is projected on the Tibetan Plateau. 
The growing risks make co-operation more urgent. But past efforts by India and China to work together on Himalayan environmental issues have made little progress. 
The two Asian powers have often found common ground at UN climate negotiations, pushing back against Western demands for emissions cuts and arguing that developing countries should not bear the same burden as industrialised nations. 
Yet they have no dedicated agreement to jointly address the impacts of climate change in the Himalayas. 
In 2009, India and China agreed to undertake joint research into the impact of global warming on glaciers in the Himalayas and Tibet. 
Following a visit to Beijing, India's then environment minister Jairam Ramesh announced that the Wadia Institute of Himalayan Geology and China's Cold and Arid Regions Environmental and Engineering Research Institute would collaborate on the project. 
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
Hundreds of people were killed in the deadly flood that tore through the China-Nepal border in August 
But the initiative went nowhere, according to a scientist involved in the effort. 
"One meeting was held between us and the Chinese side and that was it, nothing came out of it," said Dr DP Dobhal, a retired glaciologist who headed the glaciology programme at the Wadia Institute. 
"What happened after that no one knows," he added. 
Since the early 2000s, India and China had agreements under which Beijing provided flood-season hydrological data on the Brahmaputra and Sutlej, two major rivers originating in Tibet. 
But in August 2025, India's junior foreign minister Kirti Vardhan Singh told parliament that both agreements had expired. China had stopped sharing data on the Brahmaputra in June 2023, while India had received no data on the Sutlej since 2022. 
China has not publicly explained the latest interruption. But when it withheld similar information in 2017, amid a tense military stand-off with India, Beijing blamed technical problems at its hydrological monitoring stations in Tibet, Singh said. 
Some analysts see a glimmer of hope in the recent thaw between India and China, marked by high-level political engagement and moves to revive cross-border trade through Himalayan routes. 
"These developments suggest there might be more room for the three countries to explore climate-related co-operation," says William Yang, senior analyst for North East Asia at the International Crisis Group. 
But he says Beijing is likely to remain cautious about any major agreement with India and Nepal, as border disputes remain unresolved. 
One major obstacle is that information vital for understanding climate risks can also have military value. 
"What climate scientists might see as essential research data might look like strategic intelligence to the national security establishment in an environment where two militaries face each other across a disputed frontier," says Walter Ladwig, an associate fellow in the Indo-Pacific Programme at the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI), a UK-based defence and security think tank. 
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
Experts have raised concerns over climate-related risks as the Himalayan snow cover melts rapidly 
Such tensions have also hampered past efforts to tackle disasters that cross Himalayan borders. 
The Kathmandu-based International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD) has spent more than three decades promoting regional co-operation, including on flood early-warning systems. But progress has been slow. 
"There are certain highly sensitive issues in transboundary matters like comprehensive data of river flows that countries might not want to share, particularly upstream countries," says Arun Bhakta Shrestha, a former senior specialist at ICIMOD. 
He says countries should instead focus on sharing less sensitive information about disaster risks. 
Dr Uday Kala, head of the Centre for Climate Change and Disaster Management at India's IIT Mandi, suggests starting with practical steps - jointly identifying high-risk glacial lakes and cross-border hazards, agreeing on basic data-sharing protocols and monitoring standards, and exchanging critical warnings without delay. 
"Climate change is moving the baseline itself; catching up with the previous disaster is no longer enough. We need to anticipate the next one," he says. 
Whether India and China are willing to take even these steps remains uncertain. 
For Nepal, the challenge is to convince its two powerful neighbours to put aside their differences and work together to tackle a shared climate threat.

articles.title: 'I'd talk to the TV': The paid companions bringing warmth to China's lonely
articles.summary: As loneliness grows in China, a new industry is emerging to provide companionship and support.
articles.full_text:
Figure caption, 
Watch: Why the lonely in China are hiring 'temporary children' By Stephen McDonell 
China correspondent 
- Published 13 October 2026 
"The biggest difficulty really was the loneliness. Sometimes, if I wanted to talk to someone I'd talk to the TV." 
Yang, 91, lives on the outskirts of China's bustling capital Beijing. Following the death of her husband, she was so lonely that she says she even considered the possibility of voluntary euthanasia. 
"I asked my son about it but he told me it was banned. I told him that if it ever becomes legal I want to do it - I didn't want to live any longer." 
Suffering glaucoma, with failing eyesight, she was unable to even do basic things like adjust the controls on her air conditioner. 
Cases such as Yang's have become increasingly common in Chinese cities which Associate Professor Teresa Kuan, from the Chinese University of Hong Kong, says is "exacerbated by the structure of society and the modes by which people interact". 
There are many causes of isolation in China. Like when rural migrants pursue economic opportunities, leaving behind close-knit support networks for urban centres where loneliness and uncertainty can be difficult to overcome, or when graduates uproot themselves chasing employment on the other side of the country. 
Image caption, 
Suffering from glaucoma and failing eyesight, 91-year-old Yang found simple tasks and daily life increasingly difficult on her own. 
But now a growing "loneliness industry" has emerged to try to fill these gaps in people's lives. 
Yang says her life has been transformed by one of these services - Wang Yingwei and his electric scooter delivery team - who started coming over twice a day with hot meals but whose help extends far beyond that. 
"We see ourselves as community children," Yingwei told the BBC. "It means putting yourself in the shoes of older people and carefully considering their needs. 
"For example, they may be drinking tap water which can be cloudy and contain a lot of lime. I can fix this problem with a filtered water tank. Such a small thing can make them much happier. Maybe they can't shower because their equipment is broken. I'll buy a part, replace it and their shower is fine." 
"The elderly treat us like their children, and we treat them like our own parents," he added. 
Yingwei's services cost less than half the price of employing a caregiver. 
Image caption, 
Wang Yingwei and his small delivery team offer more than just meals, bringing human connection to elderly residents. 
The former mobile phone salesman says he started his company to help seniors remain at home without having to move into retirement facilities. He was inspired to do this after his own father-in-law, who had developed Alzheimer's, had to go into a nursing home. Yingwei said he felt that the conditions there were so sub-standard he wanted to make sure others could stay out of institutions like this for as long as possible. 
His small business currently employs four people but he says there is a possibility he will expand as demand grows. 
There is still a shortage of solid data on the size of this sector – which operators say has exploded in recent years – but securities company Sinolink valued it at around $7.4 billion in 2025. And this is only expected to grow given the trajectory of modern lifestyles. 
Zheng Ruizhi, another client of Yingwei's who lives in Beijing's northern outskirts, welcomed him at the door with a big smile. 
"After retiring, I don't have much opportunity to hang out with others," the 75-year-old, whose son lives two hours away from her, told the BBC. 
She was recovering from a recent injury which she said was making everyday tasks more difficult. 
Image caption, 
Zheng Ruizhi, 75, shares a lighthearted moment with Wang Yingwei during a home visit. 
But the arrival of Yingwei – who she calls her "dear boy" – lightened her mood. 
"I call you 'dear boy' because I am so fond of you. I genuinely like you from the bottom of my heart. I also admire and trust you. When you help me out, I don't have a single worry or fear," she told him. 
Yet the services offered by those in this sector are not limited to home visits. 
Twenty-three-year-old Liu Yanyan, for instance, works as a "medical escort". She acts as a friendly face taking clients to see the doctor, or picking up their test results or medication from city hospitals, which can be intimidatingly large and bureaucratic. 
"Some of my customers are people in their 20s who came to Beijing to build a career. They might not have friends here or feel awkward asking colleagues to accompany them because of the concept of social reciprocity in Chinese culture," she said. "If I accompanied you to a doctor's appointment for free, you might feel obligated to buy me a meal or a movie ticket afterwards." 
She said that, because of this, there are many people in modern Chinese society who tend to keep to themselves. 
"So, they hire someone like me to accompany them to the hospital. If they had to go alone, they could feel scared or anxious." 
Image caption, 
Liu Yanyan, a 23-year-old medical escort, helps clients navigate complex city hospitals. 
At the core of many businesses catering to loneliness in China is a simple offering: human connection. 
Teresa Kuan said that some people prefer the option of pouring their hearts out to a complete stranger for a fee. 
"If there is a companion you have paid for, the relationship is not exactly equal. It is a service relationship, so you don't have to deal with the unpredictability of a standard relationship. The thing about friendship is that it can be unpredictable. You don't know when someone might disappoint you. But, in a service relationship, you have a better idea of what to expect." 
Wang Zhoutao runs a hiking business to help people who want to climb China's famous mountain Huangshan in Anhui Province. 
"We provide emotional support, like cheering them up, taking their photo or telling jokes. It's really a service based on companionship," he said. 
The former soldier added that he normally hikes up the mountain with clients 10 to 15 days a month. When fully booked, this could be as many as 30 times a month. 
Image caption, 
Mountain escort Wang Zhoutao guides a client up the steep steps of Mount Huangshan. 
He gave an example of a young woman he once accompanied who felt ostracised at work. "She felt useless and wanted to prove something to herself," he said. 
"We started climbing but it was a tough trek as the weather was really hot and we were sweating a lot. There were moments she wanted to give up but I told her, 'If you quit now and can't get over this mountain how will you handle anything else in life?'. I kept encouraging her." 
After they made it all the way he said she sent him a long message of thanks describing her inner journey and expressing her gratitude. 
"The pace of life is just too fast these days. People face pressure from work, relationships and family expectations," he said. "I think my clients are mostly people who feel a void in their relationships or have suffered a setback." 
Human connection is a necessity but, in a society grappling with loneliness across generations, it has now also become a commodity. 
Back in her little Beijing flat, Yang is feeling more comfortable now that Yingwei has sorted out her problem of making the air conditioner work properly. 
"It's good to have someone around when you need it, someone you can share your innermost thoughts with," she said. 
"I did struggle with loneliness but that's been resolved now. I'm quite happy. 
"I can't lose Yingwei and the others. They've all got a good heart."

articles.title: The island where locals say data centres are taking their water
articles.summary: "Not a single drop has come through our taps for the last three months," a local tells the BBC.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
Batam's reservoirs are under pressure as the island aims to be a digital hub By Muhammad Islahuddin ,  Reporting from Batam   and   Kelly Ng ,  Reporting from Singapore 
- Published 12 October 2026 
"Water! Water!" the crowd shouted as it stormed a compound with data centres, armed with empty plastic bottles and jerry cans. 
There were about 300 of them, all residents on the Indonesian island of Batam, and they were furious that the taps at home had run dry, while the data centres in the new Nongsa Digital Park seemed to have enough water to protect their machines from overheating. 
"Not a single drop has come through our taps for the last three months... Our water supply had been reliable until the data centres came," Dewi Susanti, one of the protesters, told the BBC. 
People in her village, Bakau Serip, were now depending on tanker trucks that dispensed "dirty, cloudy and smelly" water, she said. 
Batam's water utility told the BBC it was working to improve supply, but did not comment on whether the disruption was linked to demand from the data centres. 
But BP Batam, the agency overseeing trade and industry, blamed it on a prolonged dry spell and denied allegations from locals that water meant for homes was being channelled to data centres. 
This is not the first such protest in Batam, whose shrinking reservoirs find themselves under more pressure as the island tries to transform itself into a digital hub. 
Following protests in August and September, authorities told the firms opening data centres in Batam that they must build their own desalination plants instead of relying on reservoirs for freshwater. 
But locals say they are increasingly concerned that they must now compete with servers for water. 
"Reliable data on data centre water use in Indonesia remains scarce, partly because companies treat it as proprietary information," says Agus Hasan, a professor at the Norwegian University of Science and Technology. 
"We should build [data centres] rationally, transparently, and responsibly, and insist on seeing the numbers... [Otherwise] those kept in the dark while their taps run dry will push back, and rightly so," he adds. 
Image caption, 
Batam residents protesting over water shortage 
A backlash has been building against data centres across the world, from the US to the UK to parts of Asia, as tech companies pour billions into AI infrastructure. 
People are worried about how the huge, windowless buildings might change their neighbourhoods, the constant hum of machines, the security lights that could stay on all night, and the pressure this puts on water and energy resources. 
While electricity powers the centres, the water keeps the servers from frying – engineers deploy elaborate cooling systems, which consume a lot of water. 
Research in the US suggests a typical data centre consumes around 300,000 gallons of water a day, or about as much as 1,000 US households. A larger, 50MW facility could take as much water as 2,200 households per day, and enough electricity to power 22,000 homes, according to Malaysia's central bank. 
It's unclear how much water or electricity the data centres in Batam are consuming. 
But the island routinely faces water shortages, and the levels are worse this year, possibly because of a historic "super" El Niño. 
Devoid of natural freshwater sources, Batam's 1.3 million people rely on rainwater collected in six artificial reservoirs. 
Nongsa reservoir, which supplies water to Bakau Serip, where Dewi lives, would dry up over the next month with no rainfall, simulations by local environmental non-profit group Akar Bhumi Indonesia suggest. 
"The water shortage is affecting our livelihoods... Money that should be used to buy rice is now spent on water drums," Dewi says. "My husband has to wait up overnight to get water, and then go straight to work the next morning." 
Batam's water utility had earlier said that it would consider measures like cloud seeding should the water shortage continue. When asked about the recent protests, they pointed us to earlier statements. 
Image source, BBC/ Muhammad Islahuddin Image caption, 
A view of the data centres inside Batam's Nongsa Digital Park 
Authorities in Batam have approved 10 data centres, six of which will be located in Nongsa Digital Park. Two are up and running, while a third is under construction. At least six more are currently under review for approval, BP Batam told the BBC. 
Official figures put investment in data centres on the island at more than $6.7bn (£5.1bn) as of mid-2026, spurred in part by demand from Singapore, which is just an hour away by ferry. 
Singapore paused construction of data centres in 2019, citing land and energy constraints. It lifted the ban in 2022 after introducing new efficiency standards, which prompted investors to look elsewhere. 
Singapore has long been promoting the Riau Islands, which includes Batam, and the Malaysian state of Johor as "complementary" regions. 
Quick to absorb the spillover, Johor approved data centre projects worth tens of billions. But this soon drew the ire of residents frustrated with noise, dust and water shortages. The state has since tried to regulate how much water and electricity data centres consume. 
Across the strait, Batam is just as attractive to investors – from the US, China, Australia, Singapore – because of relatively low operating costs, proximity to Singapore and connections to major subsea cable routes. 
Image source, BBC/ Muhammad Islahuddin Image caption, 
A data centre under construction in Nongsa 
Nongsa is home to a 13,000-sq-m data centre by Hong Kong-based private equity firm Gaw Capital and Indonesian developer Sinar Primera. In April, Singapore's DayOne signed a deal with an Indonesian state utility to build one of the country's largest data centres with around 450MW capacity, enough to power 350,000 average households. In June, DayOne, chip maker Nvidia and Australian AI start-up Firmus Technologies announced a 360MW "AI factory". 
By 2030, power demand from data centres in Batam is expected to cross 1,100MW, which is enough to power nearly a million homes, according to the official estimates. 
The BBC has contacted DayOne, Sinar Primera and Gaw Capital for comment. 
Meanwhile, the spate of construction is worrying locals in Batam who urged authorities to prioritise their needs. 
"Don't just sit at the top and keep approving these projects. Come down here and see for yourselves what we are wrestling with," says Marlinda, who lives in the district of Sei Beduk, which is also facing water shortages. 
"We want the government to pay attention to ordinary people," another resident told the BBC. 
"Don't make billion-rupiah investments while ordinary people are made to suffer... We are not asking for anything extravagant. We just want our water supply restored."

articles.title: Netflix to shed 1,000 jobs in steepest cuts since 2022
articles.summary: The cuts equate to around 6% of the streaming giant's total workforce worldwide.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Mario Tama / Getty Images By Tom Espiner Business reporter 
- Published 14 October 2026 
Netflix has said it will cut 1,000 jobs globally as the streaming giant faces competition from rivals. 
The cuts - the steepest since 2022 - will mainly affect its human resources, legal, product and technology teams and equates to around 6% of its total workforce. 
Last month, Netflix 's co-chief executive, Ted Sarandos, told the Bloomberg Screentime summit that the company was "not growing as fast as I want us to". 
The streaming industry is going through a period of consolidation following Paramount's $110bn (£83.6bn) merger with Warner Bros, the owner of HBO, while free platforms such as YouTube and TikTok continue to attract viewers. 
In an email to staff, Sarandos and co-chief executive Greg Peters said Netflix would "continue to invest aggressively in high-impact areas to improve our service and further drive growth and innovation". 
Netflix had come close to its own deal with Warner Bros but was outbid in the end by Paramount . 
Commenting on the "organisational changes", Sarandos and Peters said: "Our mission - to entertain the world - is ambitious, and delivering on it requires us to be disciplined about where we prioritise our people and resources." 
Managers will tell employees whether their job has been cut "soon". 
Image source, Netflix Image caption, 
TV series Below, starring Josh Hartnett, is one of Netflix's most popular shows 
The email added that the firm was on track to meet its financial forecasts. The streaming service is due to report its latest results on 20 October. 
Investors have been weighing up user engagement - the amount of time customers spend on Netflix - as it competes with platforms such as YouTube and TikTok. 
The firm has continued to commission shows - its most popular at the moment is "Below", an underwater mystery series. 
It has also been attempting to expand its business, including gaming and allowing adverts to play before and during shows and films. 
However, "they haven't been able to find another line of major revenue," said Ross Benes, senior analyst at eMarketer. 
He added that the company remains reliant on a subscription business that could be approaching a plateau. 
"Eventually, because they're nearing a ceiling with that, they'll need another revenue stream to diversify, and that's where it's been more of a struggle," he said. 
The last major redundancy round at Netflix was in 2022, when it cut about 450 jobs after losing subscribers for the first time in more than a decade.

articles.title: Container ship hit by projectile sinks in Strait of Hormuz, Singapore says
articles.summary: All 21 sailors on the Singapore-flagged GFS Pride were evacuated safely after it was hit by an projectile on Tuesday, maritime authorities say.
articles.full_text:
Image source, AFP Image caption, 
The China-flagged container shipping vessel Hui Fa off Khor Fakkan, in the Gulf of Oman, on Tuesday By David Gritten 
- Published 8 hours ago 
A Singapore-flagged container ship has sunk after being struck by an unknown projectile while transiting the Strait of Hormuz, according to Singaporean authorities. 
All 21 crew members of GFS Pride were evacuated and no injuries were reported after the attack on Tuesday, which caused damage and a fire, the Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore said. 
Another Singapore-flagged container vessel, GFS Giselle, sustained hull damage after being hit by a projectile on Wednesday but was able to reach a safe anchorage with all 22 crew, it added. 
Iran's Revolutionary Guards said a ship hit naval mines and sank while passing through what they called an "unauthorised" route in the Strait of Hormuz. 
The Guards released photos that appeared to show a plume of black smoke rising from a container vessel that was still afloat but down by the stern. In other photos, dozens of containers and their contents could be seen floating in the water. 
The Hydrographer of Pakistan warned mariners that GFS Pride had sunk 4 nautical miles (7.4km) north-west of Ras al-Sheikh Masud in Oman's Musandam Peninsula. 
Meanwhile, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) agency said that two unnamed container ships had reported being struck by unknown projectiles while transiting the Strait of Hormuz between 16:40 and 17:00 GMT on Tuesday. 
Both vessels sustained minor damage and were able to continue their passages, it added. 
Merchant vessels have come under repeated attack in the Strait of Hormuz - which connects the Gulf to the Gulf of Oman and Arabian Sea - and elsewhere in the Middle East since the US and Israel's war with Iran began in February. 
At least 24 seafarers have been killed in 106 confirmed incidents, according to the UN's International Maritime Organization. 
The Malta-flagged container ship Safeen Prestige, which was attacked near Oman on 4 March, is the only other vessel reported to have sunk in that time. 
However, maritime risk management group Vanguard said on Wednesday that the Antigua and Barbuda-flagged bulk carrier Cape Dao was reported to be sinking after an unsuccessful rescue attempt, according to Reuters news agency. 
One seafarer was killed when the Cape Dao's bridge and accommodation area were hit by an unknown projectile as it transited through the Strait of Hormuz, north-east of Khasab, Oman, on 23 September. 
The Strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of global oil and gas shipments usually pass, was effectively closed after the start of the Iran war due to Iranian missile and drone attacks on commercial vessels and a US naval blockade of Iranian ports. 
The US and Iran reached a preliminary agreement to end the war and reopen the strait in June, but it collapsed within weeks after Iranian attacks on shipping resumed and the US reinstated its blockade. 
Iran insisted it would not give up some measure of control over the waterway and began targeting vessels using a southern route through Omani waters that avoids its preferred route through Iranian waters. 
To keep exports flowing from Gulf Arab states, the US military has been providing protection for tankers shuttling oil through the Strait of Hormuz. 
Last month, crude exports through the waterway rose to around 80% of pre-war levels of 16 million barrels per day (bpd) on average, according to analysts from shipping data company Kpler, despite an increase in attacks on shipping.

UK’s ‘incoherent’ approach to China plagued by lack of expertise, report says
International alliance of China-sceptic legislators warns of risks inherent in misjudging bilateral relationship 
The UK’s approach to China is “beset by incoherence” and plagued by a lack of senior expertise, according to a report warning of the risks inherent in misjudging the bilateral relationship. 
An audit by the Inter-Parliamentary Alliance on China (Ipac), an international grouping of China-sceptic legislators, says past engagement with Beijing has often exposed the UK to the risks of interference without delivering the opportunities promised. 
“Successful UK engagement with China must always be framed by an understanding that the PRC (People’s Republic of China) is an inherently hostile authoritarian state that does not share our values,” an underlined sentence in the audit, published on Wednesday, reads. 
The inherent power imbalance in the relationship with the world’s second largest economy is “further compounded by muddled policy and weak engagement”, it says. UK car industry faces ‘difficult trade-off’ between Chinese and EU markets 
Read more 
It cites the example of a visiting Chinese delegation who had noted that no one who engaged with Beijing at a senior level in government was a Mandarin speaker, or had significant experience of living in China. 
Although British expertise exists, it is often siloed and “not translated into capability”, says Ipac, pointing to budget cuts as an additional problem. 
Ipac counts almost 50 MPs among its members, including from Labour, the Conservatives, the Liberal Democrats, the Scottish National party, the Greens and Reform. 
Ipac member and former security minister Tom Tugendhat said the report was “a clear-eyed and realistic take on the defining foreign policy problem of this century, filling a gap left by years of policy neglect”. 
A UK government spokesperson said that while working with China presented opportunities, “we are also clear-eyed about the threats China poses, and national security is the first duty of government”. 
“We will cooperate with China where we can while meeting any challenges head-on,” they added. 
The Chinese embassy in London said Ipac’s “sole agenda is to manufacture falsehoods, mislead the public, and undermine China’s relations with other countries”. 
The report “distorts the facts” and “is not even worth refuting”, it added. 
While the Ipac report accepts that “disengagement is not an option”, it advocates for clearly defined red lines around issues such as critical infrastructure, frontier technologies and human rights. 
The document offers several recommendations, including better institutional coordination, the strengthened use of national security tools, and diversification of supply chains. 
Emerging technologies such as AI represent “another front we’re potentially facing”, Labour’s Dame Meg Hillier said at the launch, with the report identifying areas of concern such as disinformation and surveillance capabilities. skip past newsletter promotion 
after newsletter promotion 
The climate crisis is identified as a low-risk area for cooperation and alignment. 
“Climate targets as set will not be met without cooperation with China, and accepting medium-term dependence. This means accepting supply chains tainted by forced labour and unfair trade practices,” the audit says. 
The government conducted its own audit of the UK-China relationship in late 2024 but has said it cannot publish most of the detail for fear of damaging national interests. 
But Evan Fowler, author of the Ipac report, said that a public audit was important “because engagement with China doesn’t just happen at the government level”. 
It was “very welcome” that there was an understanding that better language skills were needed to deal with China, said Kerry Brown, a former diplomat and director of the Lau China Institute at King’s College London. 
However, he said, “the critical issue now is lived experience” in China. 
“Some of the members of Ipac … are really keen on promoting this very security-oriented idea that going to China is in some ways opening you up to exposure,” he said. 
“You can’t teach really important things in a classroom; you can only go and learn them through daily life … and that is the thing that is very difficult to do now, and it’s also the thing that doesn’t seem to be supported.”

Excluding UK from ‘Made in Europe’ law will hurt entire EU car industry, Mercedes boss warns
Ola Källenius says it will ‘weaken the industry on both sides’ ahead of act intended to counter non-EU competition 
Locking the UK out of the EU’s flagship industrial “Made in Europe” legislation would amount to a “deliberate choice” by EU leaders to “hurt” the car industry across the bloc, the head of Mercedes-Benz has said. 
Speaking in his capacity as president of the European Automobile Manufacturers’ Association (ACEA), Ola Källenius said such a move would “weaken the industry on both sides”. 
He was speaking just weeks before political leaders hope to reach agreement on the Industrial Accelerator Act (IAA), potentially keeping the UK car industry out of key contracts in the EU. 
The act, known as the Made in Europe law, aims to protect local industry by countering competition from outside the EU. 
It is mainly aimed at China , which is now enjoying a £1bn a day trade surplus with the EU, but could cause problems for the EU’s close allies including the UK, Norway, Turkey and Switzerland. 
“It does not make any sense … We would hurt our industry in the UK and the EU. That would be a deliberate choice to worsen the competitiveness of your own [EU] industry,” Källenius said at an annual briefing in Brussels on the state of the car industry. 
“We are talking about how we industrialise more in Europe, how we build local supply chains, that is what the IAA is all about,” he added. 
Andy Burnham has been lobbying hard to get the UK included in the Made in Europe legislation but is hitting resistance, particularly from France. 
The prime minister intends to raise it at the UK-EU summit on 20 November and is hoping it is not too late, even though EU leaders are aiming for political agreement on the current text by December. 
Last month, the EU urged the UK to follow the bloc and impose tariffs on imported Chinese vehicles, which it introduced in 2024. It argued this would help the UK’s case to be included in Made in Europe as it would align more closely with the EU on key trading sectors. 
But the UK business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, said on a trip to India that this was not on the cards at the moment. skip past newsletter promotion

The ACEA is also lobbying for an urgent suspension of plans to introduce 10% tariffs on UK electric vehicles (EVs) imported to the EU, and EU EVs exported to the UK. 
“We are getting very anxious about it. The deadline is in less than three months’ time. We have our feet to the fire in terms of the tariffs. All our manufacturers are worried,” said Jonathan O’Riordan, the ACEA’s international trade director. 
The tariff schedule is written into the post-Brexit Trade and Cooperation Agreement (TCA) as a way of incentivising the industry on both sides of the Channel to speed up the production of batteries, which can represent about 45% of the cost of a new car. 
Under the TCA, car exports on both sides are tariff-free if they are mainly made in Europe, but with the EU and the UK unable to produce sufficient electric batteries to compete with China, cars exported to each other’s market would be subject to a 10% tariff from next year. 
The tariff was originally due to come into force in 2024 but was suspended for three years to give the car industry more time. 
The car industry says it needs a further two- or three-year suspension urgently. 
Meanwhile, concern has intensified in the EU in the last three months over China’s trade surplus with the bloc, with a threat of trade barriers leading to an agreement on Friday between Beijing and Brussels to reduce sales of hybrid electric cars by half over four years. 
One official said the time to rebalance trade by increasing EU exports was gone. “No amount of champagne [exports] is going to revitalise the relationship [with China],” a senior EU official told a separate trade policy briefing in Brussels.

articles.title: UK resists EU pressure to hit China with tariffs
articles.summary: Exclusive: Business secretary says he will not change trade rules due to EU pressure and denies UK will become a ‘back door’ for cheap importsThe business secretary has hit back at European demands for British tariffs on Chinese imports, saying the government will not change its trade rules because of pressure from Brussels.Jonathan Reynolds warned that the government would not bow to calls from other countries for the UK to hit Chinese vehicles with import taxes, despite political pressure to align with the EU in exchange for deeper future economic ties. View image in fullscreen

UK resists EU pressure to hit China with tariffs
Exclusive: Business secretary says he will not change trade rules due to EU pressure and denies UK will become a ‘back door’ for cheap imports 
The business secretary has hit back at European demands for British tariffs on Chinese imports, saying the government will not change its trade rules because of pressure from Brussels. 
Jonathan Reynolds warned that the government would not bow to calls from other countries for the UK to hit Chinese vehicles with import taxes, despite political pressure to align with the EU in exchange for deeper future economic ties. 
The EU imposed tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles in 2024 and last Friday agreed a 350,000 a year quota on Chinese hybrid cars amid fears cheaper alternatives are causing deindustrialisation and job losses. 
Reynolds conceded that levying sanctions on Chinese goods was an option in the future, but he dismissed concerns from Brussels that the UK could provide a back door to the European market. 
His comments highlight the divisions that remain between the UK and EU on trade and industrial policy, which could derail the prime minister’s attempts to move closer to Brussels. 
“I just want to be clear: when we make any trade decision in terms of trade defence tariffs in relation to the EU, that’s based on the UK interest – it’s not based on any other country asking for that,” said Reynolds during a trade trip to India. 
“In 2024, [we] looked at this issue carefully, and we keep it under review depending on what the needs of industry are … But it comes down to what is the fundamental nature of the UK automotive sector. It’s an export-led sector, so that’s what I’ve got to take into account.” 
With Europe having imposed tariffs of up to 45% on Chinese electric cars, some believe that the UK has opened an alternative route into the EU for Chinese companies setting up in the UK to sell into the bloc. 
Nissan, for instance, has agreed to look at building cars in northern England for the Chinese manufacturer Chery . 
Reynolds rebutted those accusations, however, saying: “The UK currently has no major Chinese manufacturer based in its automotive sector, so we’re not making vehicles here and sending them to the single market through some sort of back door.” 
His comments raise the stakes ahead of intense final weeks of negotiations before the long-awaited UK-EU summit, which Andy Burnham confirmed this week would be held in Brussels on 20 November. 
The prime minister told the Commons on Monday he wanted a “serious dialogue” over the UK’s place in Europe, as he framed the summit as a possible first step to EU membership. 
The new Made in Europe trade rules aim to protect European companies from subsidised Chinese imports, but British manufacturers worry they will also be shut out of supply chains. 
The issue will not formally be on the agenda at the November summit, but British officials are hoping to use those talks to shape the European legislation. 
Diplomats on both sides of the Channel say the summit will now be an early test of whether Burnham’s desire for a “real reset” in UK-EU relations is likely to bear fruit. 
One EU official said this week that the UK’s negotiating position would determine whether it was worth pursuing more fundamental changes such as British access to the single market, a new customs union or re-accession. 
Some in Brussels have been pushing for Britain to levy tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles in return for getting access to the European market under the new trade rules. 
Reynolds has previously dismissed such an option in part because of the risk that Beijing could hit the UK with reciprocal tariffs, damaging British companies such as Jaguar Land Rover. 
He said it would be to Europe’s detriment if it did not admit the UK into the scheme. “If you look at the impact analysis of such a policy, the consequences for the EU [of] excluding the UK are much more difficult,” he said. 
“This is not just in the UK’s interest; it’s not in the EU’s interest because obviously we have integrated supply chains.” 
Reynolds said the summit was an important milestone in EU-UK relations but also insisted that new trading terms for electricity, emissions and food and drink products would be a major achievement in themselves. 
Speaking from a two-day trade delegation to Delhi and Mumbai, he acknowledged that the landmark free trade agreement he helped strike last year with India would become defunct if Britain does rejoin the EU. 
“Obviously, if you enter those arrangements, you are doing things collectively. So there would be trade relationships with the UK that were based on Europe, the EU as a whole – that is how the European Union works in terms of its relationship. 
“That’s why obviously when we were part of it, we didn’t have these separate bespoke arrangements.” 
But he insisted that it remained worth continuing to push to broaden the scope of the agreement, as he unveiled a series of UK-India investments which officials say are worth over £1bn to the UK over the next 15 years. 
The deal has already begun to reduce the price of Scotch whisky in Indian shops, after tariffs were reduced from 150% to 75%. Now British officials are keen to free up trade in services as well as goods, for example, pushing for both countries to recognise each other’s legal qualifications. 
“There are some specific things regarding who can practice law and in which area,” Reynolds said. “I am confident over the medium to long term that this will improve over time.” 
He added: “We’ve got to be cognisant of this long-term position with the EU. But frankly, there’s a job to be done here and now, which we’re doing.”

Graduate student accused of poisoning colleague and trying to flee to China arrested at LAX
Microbiologist Aili Wang, 32, poisoned tea of colleague in Wyoming who had pending patents, prosecutors allege 
A Wyoming microbiology graduate student from China has been arrested on accusations she poisoned the tea of a colleague who had pending patents and with whom she did not get along, then tried to flee the country after police questioned her. 
Aili Wang, 32, was arrested 6 October at Los Angeles international airport, where prosecutors allege she sought to return to China . With her were laptops, electronic storage devices and documents now in the possession of police, who allege Wang was seen on surveillance video rummaging through the desk of the victim who specialized in technology for disease treatment – research similar to work she had done in China. 
Wang remained jailed without bail on Tuesday in Los Angeles. She allegedly bought a chemical, acrylamide, over eBay, and it was first detected when the alleged victim’s wife and others tested water from the coffee maker he used to brew tea. 
US officials for years have accused China of stealing intellectual property from American universities. 
The microbiology professor overseeing both graduate students, Mark Gomelsky, said the accusations left him reeling. He was uncertain if the victim will fully recover. 
“It’s been disheartening, to say the least, to see that one of your students’ lives is in jeopardy and another student may be responsible for that,” Gomelsky told the Associated Press. “That was one of the worst shocks in my professional career.” 
Wang had no attorney listed in court documents. The AP tried to reach her via email and LinkedIn messages. 
The police investigation began after the victim, identified in court documents as “KT”, began experiencing symptoms and his wife and others allegedly isolated the chemical in the coffee maker water. The victim and campus police then set up surveillance cameras in the office space he shared with Wang at the university in Laramie. 
Wang allegedly was recorded 27 September going through the alleged victim’s desk. On 1 October, she was recorded “taking photos and manipulating notebooks” on his desk, as well as rinsing out his mug with a liquid from her own mug, a University of Wyoming campus police officer’s affidavit said. 
Wang and the alleged victim, who did not share research areas, did not get along, according to the affidavit. 
The alleged victim began experiencing extreme tiredness, inability to sleep and other unexplained symptoms soon after attending a prestigious conference in August, Gomelsky said. 
He also noticed a strange taste in the tea that he made with a small coffee maker on his desk, Gomelsky said. When he washed the coffee maker, Gomelsky said, the taste would go away. 
Suspecting someone in their shared office could be poisoning the graduate student, Gomelsky said a chemistry professor tested the water and identified acrylamide. 
Wang faces a felony aggravated assault and battery charge in Wyoming punishable by up to 10 years in prison and a $10,000 fine. 
It is not clear when she could be extradited to the state, where Albany county circuit court judge Robert Sanford granted prosecutors’ request and raised bond to $1.5m cash-only. 
Wang allegedly asked eBay to delete her account after she bought acrylamide over the online retail site twice last summer, police said.
